Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.

title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding
summary: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks

title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: 29 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables, Under review at Artificial Intelligence Review
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
summary: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, including references and appendices. Benchmark website: https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/
summary: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
summary: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
summary: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
summary: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
summary: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure
comment: 23 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Code available at https://github.com/Elyasirankhah/PTI
summary: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

title: ListQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating List-Formatted Factual Knowledge Retrieval in Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project Page: https://listqa.github.io
summary: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.

title: Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation
summary: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

title: Verification Turns Capability Gaps into Routing Decisions: Small Language Models for Clinical Documentation
summary: Clinical note generation from doctor--patient dialogue is high-volume and hallucination-intolerant: a fabricated laboratory value can create patient-safety risk, not a quality regression. We ask whether an agentic \emph{verification} architecture, rather than generator scale, can make a small language model viable here. Holding a four-evaluator verification stack and refinement policy fixed and swapping only the generator between a 4B-parameter model with a QLoRA adapter and a frontier baseline, the small model reaches $0.984$ claim-level factual entailment against $0.992$ and comes within $3.3$ points on completeness, generating entirely on-device. Its deficit is confined to \emph{inter-section structural fidelity}---arrangement rather than clinical comprehension, and the axis on which it also falls furthest below the corpus's reference notes. Because that deficit is an explicit verifier decision rather than a silent quality difference, it becomes a routing policy: run the small model by default, escalate what the verifier rejects. Measured end to end, that it achieved a similiar verified-rate acceptance to the frontier-only acceptance in this test set ($99.6\%$ vs.\ $98.4\%$ over $250$ encounters) while routing $62$, documenting three quarters without a frontier \emph{generation} call. Ablating the loop separates architecture from scale: unrefined, the small model is accepted on $26.8\%$ of encounters and the frontier model on $74.8\%$, so verification does the most work where the generator is weakest. We also contribute section-scoped refinement, which preserves unflagged sections by construction rather than instruction, and find the baseline is not uniformly stronger---its provider refused two trauma-related transcripts the on-device model handled and certified, one facet of a provider dependency a served adapter does not carry.

title: Learning from Self-Generated Responses: Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation for Reasoning
summary: Reference solutions and question-specific rubrics are not always available to guide the teacher in self-distillation. A large language model's own solution attempts offer an alternative, but their quality is difficult to assess in open-ended tasks without automatic correctness checks, and even correct attempts can involve uncertain token predictions. We propose Reliability--Uncertainty Self-Distillation (\method{}) to learn from these attempts. The same model serves as teacher and student: the teacher receives the question and completed attempt, and the student matches the teacher's token-level predictions using a question-only prompt. \method{} weights each attempt's distillation loss by additively combining judged reliability, estimated from a self-judge's score and confidence, with student predictive uncertainty. Across eleven reasoning benchmarks, \method{} outperforms all five baselines in average accuracy, reaching 70.47\% on Qwen3-4B and 76.69\% on Qwen3-8B (8.90 and 2.10 percentage points above the base models). Data and code are available at https://github.com/JP-25/RUSD.

title: Multi-System Cognitive Steering for Generative Communication
summary: A fundamental bottleneck for translating thoughts to speech is the high physical cost of motor input forcing a strict tradeoff between communication speed and expressivity. Generative AI offers a promising solution by expanding highly abbreviated text input into fluent sentences, significantly reducing the motor burden on the user. However, sparse inputs are inherently ambiguous; without sufficient context, AI models frequently misinterpret these abbreviations and generate outputs that fail to align with the user's true cognitive intent. We propose \textit{Cognitive Steering}, a framework that can be leveraged to reconstruct user intent by grounding Large Language Models (LLMs) in multimodal context and applying AI control methods. We demonstrate that aligning frontier models with selected environmental referents, emotional states, and communication motives on simulated abbreviation benchmarks achieves up to $\sim$88\% top-5 expansion accuracy, doubling no-context baselines. We also reveal that different types of context require distinct AI control techniques: while physical objects in a scene are best provided through explicit text prompts, abstract factors like emotion may be more effectively managed by directly altering the AI's internal activations. These findings suggest a hybrid architecture for future interfaces that leverage Cognitive Steering to help users communicate both quickly and accurately, recruiting multiple AI control methods simultaneously to perfectly capture their intended communication goals.

title: HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation
summary: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

title: Adaptive Computation with Conformal Certification
summary: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.

title: NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis
summary: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

title: Titan-Llama: Retrofitting Pre-trained LLMs with External Neural Memory Modules
summary: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}

title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
summary: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

title: REPORT-OPS: Hybrid Evidence-Guided Reporting with Human-Supervised Refinement for HPC
comment: Konate and Akewar contributed equally to this work
summary: Operational reporting for high-performance computing (HPC) facilities requires combining information from monitoring services, schedulers, incident and maintenance records, storage measurements, periodic reports, and operator investigations. Producing a reliable report requires more than retrieving relevant records: the evidence must refer to the correct system, metric definition, time period, and source of authority. We present REPORT-OPS, a hybrid reporting agent in which an LLM interprets requests, plans evidence collection, evaluates possible explanations, and drafts reports, while author-seeded operational policies and automated checks determine whether the available evidence supports the requested conclusion. Depending on the evidence state, the system answers the request, reports a qualified conclusion, or withholds an unsupported claim. During offline refinement, an LLM critic proposes bounded policy changes that a human approves or rejects without editing; accepted candidates are promoted only after automated target, held-out, and regression testing. We evaluate REPORT-OPS on 68 sanitized reporting queries constructed from 50 base scenarios in a frozen HPC operational corpus, using three agent models and two LLM judges. REPORT-OPS achieves 68.63% Pass@80, compared with 7.02% for the strongest retrieval baseline. Evidence gating increases claim-support precision from 40.58% to 90.06%. On the 13-query explanatory subset, explanation accuracy reaches 55.54%. Across five rounds of human-supervised refinement, localized policy updates correct 91.17% of targeted failures and improve performance on related held-out cases by 9.33 percentage points, with no observed regression breaks under release gating. These results demonstrate improved evidence-grounded reporting and within-environment policy reuse; they do not establish unrestricted causal discovery or cross-facility generalization.

title: Definition Grounding in Theory-Level Auto-formalization
summary: LLM-based auto-formalization systems can now generate formally verified Lean code at unprecedented rates. However, a formalization advances mathematical research only when further mathematical results can be built on it, especially when its definitions and helper lemmas are general enough to be imported and used idiomatically. We propose definition grounding, where definition formalizations are continuously judged and revised, as a method to ensure formalization quality. We find that agents formalizing definitions from textbook text often produce definitions that later statements cannot use, and only 25%-50% of their definition sets are compatible with all later statements. However, clarifying the informal definitions can improve this rate up to 77.5% averaged over all models. Furthermore, stating a small set of basic properties without proving them can improve model judges' capability to detect definitions with compatibility issues, at only about 11% of the definition formalization cost. These results are verified with ReuseBench, a benchmark we curated for formalizing new mathematical fields and theories.

title: FinGREAT: Evaluating LLMs on Financial Graph-guided Retrieval And Typing
summary: Financial disclosures express the underlying relationships of double-entry accounting through unstructured text. While financial LLM benchmarks predominantly emphasize question answering and classification, schema-guided evidence discovery remains relatively under-explored. We investigate whether open-weight LLMs can extract and classify evidence corresponding to predefined double-entry accounting relationships underlying the text. Using a financial accounting graph comprising 11 nodes (accounts) and 11 edges (transaction types), we evaluate mid-sized models from 5 open-weight families across 1,300 SEC 10-K Item 7 filings spanning 26 years, comparing their extraction performance against three proprietary models. Results reveal substantial differences in extraction volume, edge distributions, and cross-model agreement. Building on this study, we introduce a human-annotated relation classification benchmark comprising 483 passages across three financial accounting categories, evaluating 34 open-weight and 10 proprietary models. The strongest open-weight and proprietary models achieve 84.1\% and 92.8\% accuracy, respectively, with considerable variation across accounting categories. Our findings highlight the importance of evaluating evidence discovery and relation understanding separately, while investigating locally deployable models for scalable, privacy-sensitive financial analysis.

title: MemeTrace: A Multimodal LLM-Based Agent for Safety-Aware Meme Provenance Analysis
summary: Online memes are often carriers of unsafe content such as disinformation and propaganda. Their rapid evolution in response to news events and strong dependence on contextual information make it difficult for platforms and moderators to detect and moderate them effectively. Moreover, existing moderation studies typically classify memes as safe or unsafe based on individual images, lacking the ability to perform broader provenance analysis, i.e., where a meme originates, how it spreads, what cultural symbolism it represents, whether it poses potential risks to society, etc. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemeTrace, a multimodal LLM-based agent that automatically traces the provenance and potential risks of emerging memes. We evaluate MemeTrace on Meme100, a dataset of 100 real-world memes, using both human annotation and automatic metrics. The results demonstrate that MemeTrace substantially outperforms the VLM baseline. More importantly, MemeTrace achieves higher accuracy in detecting unsafe memes, especially those involving disinformation and sensitive content, and remains robust under visual perturbations.

title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
summary: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.

title: Exact Scaling Laws for a Random-Features Bigram Model
summary: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.

title: Kandinsky S2V 1.0: Audio-Driven Avatar Video Generation
comment: Technical report on the open-source S2V model
summary: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide π-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

title: Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance
summary: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

title: Data-free Multistep Diffusion Distillation
summary: One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64x64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512x512, while requiring 4-5x less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.

title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
summary: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

title: SonoWorld: Towards Interactive Pose-Controllable Ultrasound World Models
summary: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

title: NavAble: A Large-Scale Dataset and Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Blind Navigation
summary: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

title: Beyond Initial Creation: Two Decades of Community-based Chart Revisions from Wikimedia Commons
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, accepted by IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Open online communities like Wikipedia offer a rich space for understanding the organic evolution of public-facing artifacts, but little is known about how these communities collectively edit chart images. We investigate the phenomenon of "community editing" of visualizations by exploring chart revision patterns on Wikimedia Commons. We introduce a novel dataset of 7,786 longitudinal chart revisions across 1,664 images, labeled with edit categories using an LLM pipeline. Initial data analysis uncovered several novel findings. Multi-contributor revision is associated with more edits to mark styling and text content compared to single-contributor revision. Temporally, mark and text edits occur in more "bursty" cadences than data edits. In addition, while SVG charts attract more unique contributors and revisions than raster charts, their edit histories involve more tightly scoped and less diverse changes. This dataset enables a wide range of analyses of chart change over time.

title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
summary: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.

title: Integrated Novelty Detection Systems: From Sensor Networks to Multi-Novelty Computer Vision
summary:
Novelty detection is crucial in various technological and scientific domains. Its importance spans from ensuring the reliability of sensor networks to enhancing the adaptability of computer vision systems. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and complex, effective anomaly detection is essential for maintaining reliability and accuracy. This work addresses novelty detection in weather sensor networks and computer vision. In weather sensor networks, particularly for monitoring rainfall, detecting blocked rain gauges can significantly impact data reliability, food security, and disaster management. This work evaluates four existing quality control methods for detecting blocked rain gauges and demonstrates their limitations, particularly in detecting clusters of faulty sensors. By comparing methods such as the Conditional Mixture Model (CMM), PSWQ (Fz-filter), Kernel Regression, and Gaussian Method, we identify their shortcomings and propose three novel quality control techniques that integrate probabilistic fault detection and consistency-based diagnosis framework to improve timely detection of blocked sensors, while reducing false alarms.
  In the realm of computer vision, current systems often fail to handle multiple types of novelty due to their focus on single-novelty scenarios. We highlight the need for integrated systems capable of handling multiple types of novelty. To support this, we introduce the Novel Snapshot Serengeti (NOVEL-SS) dataset, derived from the Snapshot Serengeti camera trap data, which includes various forms of novelty. We also present the DCA (Detect, Characterize, and Accommodate) baseline system, designed to handle multiple novelty by detecting, characterizing, and accommodating them. This work aims to advance the robustness and adaptability of novelty detection systems across both weather sensor networks and computer vision applications.

title: Dynamic Graph World Modelling: Learning Future Dynamics from Temporal Context
summary: Dynamic graph learning models how entities and their relations evolve from historical observations to predict future graph states. Existing methods do not fully address dynamic graph world modelling, which requires learning transitions from temporal context to future latent graph states. This is difficult for three reasons: nodes and relations rely on different historical evidence, structural evolution is path-dependent, and future snapshots provide sparse and realization-specific targets. We propose Dynamic Graph World Modelling (DyG-WM), the first framework to jointly predict future node and relation representations from temporal context by answering three questions: what has evolved, how it evolved, and what will evolve next. To capture what has evolved, a historical node-relation context encoder summarizes node-neighborhood trajectories and pair-specific histories. To characterize how it evolved, a node-relation path-signature encoder captures ordered structural changes. To predict what will evolve next, a dual-level joint-embedding objective predicts target-snapshot node and relation representations without reconstructing the raw graph. Experiments on 12 link-prediction and two node-classification datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DyG-WM across both tasks.

title: The Impact of Detector Architecture, Model Scale, and Scene Density on Multi-Pedestrian Tracking
summary: Pedestrian tracking in video is important for applications such as surveillance and scene analysis, but it becomes more challenging in crowded scenarios with frequent occlusions and rapid motion. This paper analyzes how detector architecture, model scale, scene density, and inference regime affect the tracking of multiple pedestrians. We compare the YOLO11, RT-DETR, and YOLO26 detector families with the ByteTrack and BoT-SORT trackers on sequences from the MOT17, MOT20, and SOMPT22 benchmarks. For YOLO26, we also compare traditional overlap filtering via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) with end-to-end inference. The RT-DETR family achieved the highest mean scores on the HOTA tracking quality metric across all three benchmarks with both trackers, with a more pronounced advantage on MOT20, albeit at a higher computational cost. On MOT17 and SOMPT22, YOLO26 variants, especially YOLO26-L with NMS, offered favorable combinations of quality and speed compared with RT-DETR. In the YOLO26 inference comparison, the end-to-end mode did not yield consistent tracking gains over the NMS-based regime. Taken together, these results provide a practical guide for selecting detectors and trackers for this task based on application priorities.

title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables. Companion paper: arXiv:2610.11030
summary: Runtime policy verifiers can prevent agents from executing disallowed actions, but their decisions are typically used only for enforcement and discarded afterward. We ask whether these decisions can instead become verifiable policy rewards for training the agents they guard. We introduce Policy-Verified Self-Training (PVST), a post-training paradigm in which an agent generates its own interaction trajectories and an executable policy verifier, here a deterministic gate compiled from a written policy, evaluates whether each action complies. Compliant trajectories are reinforced, and violations become negatives for preference optimization; beyond the gate and the benchmark's task-success signal, PVST needs no stronger teacher model, no human preference labels and no attack-specific supervision, although rollouts are collected in the benchmark's attacked environment. On held-out AgentDojo tasks under prompt injection, policy-verified preference training of Qwen3-8B reduces violating trajectories from 37.2% to 10.3 $\pm$ 0.9% (three seeds) and successful attacks from 12.4% to 0.5% at equal or higher pooled task utility, although utility falls on travel, compared with 22.0% when negatives are selected by an attack oracle and 31.9 $\pm$ 0.9% with negatives that contain no violation. The learned behavior holds under an attack template never used in training (37.7% to 11.0%) and on a suite excluded from training (34.8% to 16.7%), and the retained verifier's intervention rate falls from 39.2% to 8.8% (seed 0). Our analysis identifies two conditions under which the verdict is most informative: success must not already imply compliance, and guarded actions must appear in both permitted and forbidden contexts.

title: Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback
summary: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

title: EvoWeave: Composing Reusable Agent Experience through Operation Level Graphs
summary: Different tasks often require interactive agents to perform similar operations at intermediate steps. Retrieving an entire past workflow can introduce irrelevant steps, whereas retrieving isolated operations can discard the dependencies needed to reuse them. We introduce EvoWeave, a framework for experience memory that represents abstract states as nodes and reusable operations as directed edges with input and output contracts, provenance, and capability references. A planner decomposes the current task into a dependency graph; operation retrieval and bounded directed search then assemble relevant experience fragments. An execution agent can inspect these fragments and their referenced capabilities, while reflection separates concrete execution evidence from reusable abstractions. We study the framework across four benchmarks, five evaluation settings, and three language model backbones. Across backbones, AppWorld Normal and Challenge task goal completion average 51.91 and 27.99, respectively, exceeding the baseline without memory by 6.99 and 4.99 percentage points. An AppWorld ablation associates directed connections with an additional improvement of 2.08 points over independent operation cards. The results motivate composition of reusable operations while exposing tradeoffs in retrieval overhead and conditions for valid reuse.

title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.

title: The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation
summary: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

title: ELARSpeech: A 30K-Hour Dataset Across 675 Underrepresented Languages for Long-Tail Multilingual Speech Technologies
summary: Massively multilingual speech modeling has made remarkable progress in recent years, yet existing training resources and benchmarks still underrepresent much of the linguistic long tail. To address this gap, we introduce ELARSpeech, a large-scale multilingual speech resource comprising 30,202 hours of speech across 675 underrepresented languages, curated from the Endangered Languages Archive. Combining human-annotated and unlabeled recordings, the corpus spans diverse recording conditions, domains, and language families. Beyond corpus construction, our experiments show how ELARSpeech supports extending ASR and TTS capabilities to diverse underrepresented languages, with further benefits from pseudo-labeling unlabeled data. At the same time, our speech representation analysis reveals remaining limitations in transferring existing multilingual models to the linguistic long tail. Together, ELARSpeech provides both a resource and a testbed for extending multilingual speech technology further into the linguistic long tail. We publicly release the dataset, all trained ASR and TTS models, and the complete data construction pipeline to facilitate research on long-tail multilingual speech technologies.

title: EpiGuard: An Autonomous Infectious-Disease Early Warning Agent Platform
summary: Infectious disease outbreaks often spread rapidly before signs of widespread transmission become apparent, leaving a big challenge for rapid response and effective intervention. However, current infectious-disease early-warning systems face three major challenges: fragmented epidemiological evidence across diverse surveillance sources, highly uneven data availability across diseases and geographic regions, and delayed warning procedure caused by manual data collection, analysis, and reporting. To address these challenges, we present EpiGuard, an autonomous, continually self-improving agentic platform for timely and reliable early warning of more than 50 infectious diseases across different regions. EpiGuard proactively monitors and captures newly released official surveillance records, using the latest available evidence for risk assessments. It dynamically adjusts its analytical strategy across three evidence availability regimes, enabling reliable risk assessment under diverse data conditions, ranging from the absence of historical observations to sparse and abundant evidence. Moreover, EpiGuard learns from the successful execution process by preserving effective data-acquisition and analytical procedures as reusable standard operating procedures, enabling it to progressively generalize to previously unseen diseases and regions. We use officially released infectious-disease surveillance data from the China CDC and the United States CDC to evaluate EpiGuard's effectiveness. Experimental results demonstrate that EpiGuard outperforms state-of-the-art forecasting systems, improving forecasting performance by 9.68% and 14.04% on the China CDC and U.S. CDC datasets, respectively.

title: SERO: Learning from Executable Oracle Continuations for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Long-horizon agentic RL is constrained by the futures visited by the current policy. When rollouts fail to reach useful behaviors, improved credit assignment cannot provide supervision for states and actions that were never encountered. On-policy distillation (OPD) introduces teacher guidance on policy-induced states, and recent multi-turn variants improve how this guidance is scheduled, replayed, refined, or validated. However, they do not directly use the oracle-controlled future itself as the training trajectory. We introduce \textbf{State-Rooted Executable Rollout Optimization (SERO)}, which augments on-policy agentic RL with executable oracle continuations. SERO restores a state actually reached by the current policy and lets a training-only oracle continue interacting with the real environment, making the downstream observations and oracle actions themselves available for learning. It then applies \textbf{policy-reachability weighting}, which weights each oracle step by the frozen behavior policy's compatibility with the preceding oracle actions. This allows deeper supervision to become effective as the policy becomes more compatible with the oracle branch. The oracle loss is optimized separately from the base RL estimator and no oracle is used at inference time. We evaluate SERO on two challenging interactive-agent benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. On ALFWorld, learning the full executable continuation is substantially more effective than supervising only the root oracle action, while policy-reachability weighting further improves out-of-distribution performance.

title: Train to Stitch: Topology-Preserving Regularization for Interoperable Representations
summary: As large, powerful pre-trained models become more prevalent, there is growing interest in developing methods that allow different neural networks to be seamlessly combined with little or no direct communication between them. Take autoencoder-based data compression as an example: the ability to independently choose architectures and train encoder and decoder models, while still ensuring they work together, could fundamentally transform how such models are built, deployed, and updated. In this work, we introduce a novel approach that leverages topological regularization to align the latent spaces of two independently trained autoencoder models, entirely eliminating the need for coordination during training. We provide a conditional theoretical analysis showing how the structural agreement encouraged by our regularizer can translate into approximate geometric compatibility between independently learned representations. Reconstruction experiments validate this approach empirically, substantially narrowing the interoperability gap across multiple datasets.

title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. The first two authors contributed equally
summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

title: W-JEPA: Wavelet Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Wearable Activity Recognition
summary: A major challenge in wearable device activity recognition is the heterogeneity across datasets in sensor placement, channel count, sampling rate and subjects. Moreover, the motion patterns that distinguish activities often appear as subtle, scale-specific variations within otherwise similar waveforms. As a result, raw signals are often ambiguous, and models trained on them tend to rely on cues specific to a particular sensor setup or participant, which limits both cross-dataset transfer and generalization to unseen participants. Addressing this requires representations that preserve such activity-relevant, scale-specific variation. We introduce W-JEPA, a self-supervised framework that exploits the multiscale structure of inertial motion and leverages a joint-embedding predictive architecture, by organizing windows into a fixed grid of wavelet tokens indexed by scale, sensor axis, and time. These wavelet tokens help expose activity-specific detail within broadly similar raw signals, and serve as the units of masked latent prediction. W-JEPA predicts masked token representations supplied by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder. Because recovering a masked token requires relating motion at one scale and axis to motion at other scales and axes, the model learns the cross-scale, cross-axis structure of human movement. Across six wearable activity benchmarks, W-JEPA outperforms state-of-the-art methods under random-window splits and remains the strongest when subjects are held out, improving average macro-F1 by 8.7 percentage points over the strongest published baseline. These results indicate that physically grounded multiscale tokenization, combined together with latent predictive learning, provides a promising foundation for transferable representations of heterogeneous wearable inertial data.

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
summary: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.

title: Evaluating Agentic Capabilities Before Post-Training: An End-to-End Approach
summary: Agentic capabilities are increasingly important for modern LLMs, yet remain difficult to evaluate during pretraining. Existing approaches typically rely on static trajectory-derived tasks or likelihood-based proxies, which are lightweight but provide limited visibility into how base models behave in interactive environments. We introduce ASAP (Agent Scaffold Adaptation for Pretraining Evaluation), a lightweight framework for eliciting and evaluating agentic behavior from pretrained base models on end-to-end tasks. Rather than converting base models into chat-style agents, ASAP preserves the completion interface and adapts existing agent scaffolds through structured trajectory continuation, short reference prefixes, and minimal recovery mechanisms. Across software-engineering and deep-research benchmarks, ASAP yields discriminative end-to-end performance across base models and pretraining checkpoints. Beyond aggregate scores, ASAP exposes model-generated execution trajectories, enabling analysis of exploration, editing, testing, recovery, and task completion across training stages. These trajectories provide a behavioral view of how agent-relevant capabilities change during pretraining and how execution patterns differ after post-training. Our results suggest that end-to-end agent evaluation can complement conventional pretraining benchmarks by providing a practical diagnostic of interactive model behavior.

title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
summary: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.
